response: Yes, anterior laxity of the uninjured knee can influence clinical outcomes of ACL reconstruction. Studies have shown that patients with increased anterior laxity in their uninjured knee may have different outcomes and rehabilitation requirements after ACL reconstruction compared to those with normal laxity. This is because the uninjured knee can serve as a reference point for the injured knee, and excessive laxity in the uninjured knee may affect the overall knee function and stability after ACL reconstruction. As a result, surgeons and physical therapists may need to consider the laxity of the uninjured knee when developing rehabilitation plans and setting expectations for patients undergoing ACL reconstruction.
